title: Free Speech and Civil Liberties
text:
Free Speech and Civil Liberties

At a Glance

The United States has a strictly limited federal government, with a robust Bill of Rights, yet our freedom of speech and civil liberties remain in question as government seeks new authority over citizens. The federal government today limits our political speech, subjects us to more wiretapping than ever before, criminalizes more activities every year, regulates and sometimes interferes with the content of broadcasting, and assumes unprecedented police and prosecutorial powers. The best way to protect civil liberties is to rein in the scope and power of the federal government and begin to return the federal government to its constitutional limits.

Private Property Shouldn’t Be Commandeered for Others’ Speech

By Thomas A. Berry and Dan Greenberg

California forces privately owned shopping malls to host pamphleteers and protesters, even when the owners disagree with the hosted speech. The Supreme Court should hold that this rule violates the First Amendment rights of property owners.

Drawing Policy Lessons from the Fox-Dominion Libel Case

By Walter Olson

Ian Rosenberg has written a new book, Terrible Stuff Damaging Everybody, about the Dominion v. Fox libel litigation and settlement. It furnishes some policy lessons. 

Commentary

9/11’s Aftereffect: The Constitutional Accountability Abyss

By Patrick G. Eddington

9/11 didn’t change us, we allowed it to change us, and in doing so critically damaged our very own political way of life.

The President’s Ban on Journalists Is Disgraceful and Illegal

By Dan Greenberg

It is a pity that Donald Trump has evidently not yet learned this important lesson, and it is unfortunately an open question what he will learn when he loses the lawsuit that CNN and others filed yesterday.

Its Spying on Cato Exposed, the FBI Wants Its Database Names Kept Secret—That’s How Rights Violations Start and Endure

By Patrick G. Eddington

A FOIA exemption meant to protect unique, perishable law enforcement tradecraft should not become the tool that keeps the public from knowing even the names of the systems being run in its name and potentially being used to track their very patterns of life, much less categorize them as de facto enemies of the state.
